claims.text: Laser-cladding a high-entropy-alloy protective coating onto high-value components will improve their surface physical and mechanical characteristics under aggressive service conditions.
Untreated 316L stainless-steel surfaces are susceptible to wear, pitting, spalling, and degradation in frictional, air, or seawater environments.
FeCoNiCrMo0.2 coatings, including variants reinforced with WC, can be deposited on 316L stainless steel by laser cladding.
Laser cladding of the proposed coating will produce strong metallurgical bonding.
Laser cladding of the proposed coating will produce a refined microstructure.
The coating is expected to remain effective during thermal exposure up to approximately 800 °C.
The coating is expected to remain effective in aqueous NaCl or simulated-seawater environments.
The coating is expected to remain effective under frictional or tribocorrosion loading.
The coating will form a dense, fine-grained HEA microstructure.
Beneficial secondary phases, including in situ protective oxides, will form in the coating.
Solid-solution strengthening will increase the coating's resistance to surface degradation.
Protective oxide layers formed during thermal exposure will improve resistance to surface degradation.
Improved microstructural homogeneity will increase resistance to surface degradation.
The HEA coating will increase surface hardness and reduce frictional material loss relative to an untreated surface.
Coated components will have reduced wear rates relative to uncoated components.
Coated components will have reduced tribocorrosion rates and improved oxidation and corrosion resistance relative to uncoated components.
Performance under temperatures well above 800 °C or extremely high salt concentrations is uncertain.
The exact improvements in hardness, wear rate, and corrosion resistance, as well as long-term cyclic-thermal durability, remain uncertain.
